Explanation: The App is the Core Value Unit: the digital product Users come to discover, install and use across Apple’s App Store, alternative marketplaces or eligible web distribution.
Apple remains the platform Owner because it owns iOS and iPadOS and controls core technical infrastructure even when an App is distributed through somebody else’s marketplace.
Apple’s job is to operate the iOS and iPadOS app platform while keeping it secure, useful to Users and attractive to Developers.
A larger app ecosystem can make Apple’s devices and operating systems more useful while generating more commercial activity and platform revenue.
Alternative marketplaces, Web Distribution and alternative payments allow more of the app-distribution and commerce journey to bypass Apple’s own App Store.

Apple provides access to the underlying platform and can charge for covered commercial activity even when distribution occurs outside its own App Store. Under the August 2026 terms, the Core Technology Commission is 5% on specified digital transactions in alternatively distributed apps beginning October 1, 2026.
Transaction Flows: ← Provider · Fee — Under the announced October 2026 terms, Developers can owe Apple a 5% Core Technology Commission on specified digital sales even when the App was distributed outside Apple’s App Store. | → Provider · Access — Apple provides Developers access to the operating-system platform, developer tools, signing, Notarization and alternative-distribution technologies. | → Partner · APIs — Apple provides authorized alternative marketplaces with MarketplaceKit APIs and system permissions required to install and manage Apps on iOS and iPadOS. | ← Partner · Reports — Alternative marketplaces and Developers report relevant outside transactions to Apple so applicable commissions can be calculated.

Explanation: The DMA constrains Apple’s ability to make its own App Store the only ordinary distribution gate, while Apple still controls technical gates such as Notarization, signing, authorization and system permissions.
Apple continues to promote Apps through its own App Store using search, rankings, featuring and discovery.
Apple signs software, runs Notarization and security checks, maintains APIs and enforces platform requirements across distribution routes.
Apple’s critical resources sit underneath competing Stores: iOS, iPadOS, developer tools, software signing and the APIs that distribution routes depend on.
The Consumer side is iPhone and iPad users in the European Union who want useful apps on the devices they already own.
Users want to get the apps they need onto their iPhone or iPad.
The DMA increases choice by giving eligible EU Users additional routes for obtaining apps beyond Apple’s own App Store.
Different distribution channels can create different support, refund, moderation, payment and trust processes for Users.
Users install apps and may pay for paid apps, digital goods or subscriptions through the commercial options supported by the chosen distribution route.
Transaction Flows: → Provider · Payment — With alternative payment options, the economic payment can go to the Developer without Apple In-App Purchase, although a third-party payment processor may technically mediate the transfer. | ← Provider · App — Developers give Users the App. The distribution source can change while the Core Value Unit stays the same. | ← Partner · Access — An alternative marketplace gives Users another route to discover and install Apps.

Explanation: Alternative distribution depends on EU eligibility, a supported iPhone or iPad, an eligible Apple account and the technical requirements of the chosen route.
EU Users can obtain notarized apps not only from Apple’s App Store but also from authorized alternative app marketplaces and, for eligible Developers, directly from a registered website.
Users find an app, choose a source, approve installation and use the app.
Users bring the Apple device and account required to participate in the iOS or iPadOS app ecosystem.
Developers are the Provider side because they create the Apps that Users want.
Developers want to reach iPhone and iPad Users and make their software economically viable.
Additional distribution and payment routes can expand reach and, depending on the chosen route, improve the economics available to Developers.
Developers want access to iPhone and iPad Users without unnecessary cost, restrictions or complex platform rules.
Developers provide the App and receive revenue when Users purchase paid Apps, digital goods or services.
Transaction Flows: ← Consumer · Payment — With alternative payment options, the economic payment can go to the Developer without Apple In-App Purchase, although a third-party payment processor may technically mediate the transfer. | → Consumer · App — Developers give Users the App. The distribution source can change while the Core Value Unit stays the same. | → Owner · Fee — Under the announced October 2026 terms, Developers can owe Apple a 5% Core Technology Commission on specified digital sales even when the App was distributed outside Apple’s App Store. | ← Owner · Access — Apple provides Developers access to the operating-system platform, developer tools, signing, Notarization and alternative-distribution technologies. | → Partner · App — A Developer can provide a notarized App to an authorized alternative marketplace for distribution.

Explanation: Apps distributed outside Apple’s App Store are still subject to Apple’s Notarization baseline review for security, privacy and platform integrity.
Developers can reach EU Users through Apple’s App Store, authorized alternative app marketplaces and, when eligible, direct Web Distribution.
Developers build, maintain and update their Apps and submit them for the checks required by the distribution route they choose.
Developers contribute code, intellectual property, content and the services behind the App.

Independent alternative app marketplaces become a meaningful external Partner layer because they can distribute Developers’ Apps to EU Users without being the App Provider or the underlying platform Owner.
Alternative Stores need to attract enough Developers and enough Users to make their marketplace useful.
Successful alternative Stores can gain scale and create their own fee or monetization models.
Alternative marketplace operators inherit responsibilities for moderation, fraud prevention, support, disputes, refunds, infrastructure and customer service.
Alternative Stores list Apps from Developers and provide Users with another route to discover and install them.

Explanation: Marketplace operators require Apple authorization and must satisfy financial, operational and platform requirements.
Alternative Stores connect through MarketplaceKit and related Apple APIs and distribute their marketplace app from an authorized website.
Marketplace operators curate Apps, support Users and Developers, handle disputes and operate the marketplace.
Alternative Stores contribute a storefront, servers, catalog infrastructure and support operations.
